Phenotypes in bronchiectasis Etiology-associated phenotypes The initial step in managing bronchiectasis is identifying the underlying cause. In some cases, the identified etiologies may serve as bronchiectasis phenotypes. Non-tuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (NTM-PD), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), and immunodeficiency are associated with targeted treatments ( 13 - 15 ). Meanwhile, rheumatoid arthritis, bronchiectasis-chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) overlap, and primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) are associated with worse outcomes or require adjustments in management ( 2 , 16 - 18 ).

However, etiology-based phenotyping presents challenges in clinical practice. The international registry data indicate that 29–41% of bronchiectasis cases are idiopathic ( 19 - 24 ). Additionally, post-infective bronchiectasis accounts for 20–27% of cases ( 19 - 24 ). The lack of specific therapies for post-infective bronchiectasis makes it clinically similar to idiopathic bronchiectasis from the clinicians’ perspectives. Therefore, approximately 70–80% of patients with bronchiectasis may gain limited benefits from etiological investigations. From a different point of view, the observed low adherence to guideline-recommended etiologic screening and incomplete diagnoses raises concerns about the reliability of these data ( 21 , 25 ). Genetic testing, which remains significantly underutilized, indicates that over 10% of patients may have PCD, providing potential insights into idiopathic or post-infective bronchiectasis ( 17 ) (discussed further below). Improving the accuracy of etiological diagnoses and conducting in-depth research on the pathogenesis of bronchiectasis could advance etiology-based management strategies and ultimately improve patient care and outcomes.

Non-tuberculous mycobacteria pulmonary disease phenotype Among the etiology-associated phenotypes, we aimed to highlight NTM-PD. The association between bronchiectasis and NTM-PD is well-known ( 26 - 28 ), and approximately 13% of patients with bronchiectasis were diagnosed with NTM-PD in a Southern European bronchiectasis registry ( 29 ). Yang et al. used a Korean nationwide 10-year follow-up dataset and revealed that the incidence of NTM-PD in those with bronchiectasis was approximately 19-fold higher than that in patients without bronchiectasis, even after adjusting for various confounding factors ( 30 ).

What clinical features can aid in identifying NTM-PD in patients with bronchiectasis? NTM-PD is disproportionally more prevalent in women, and its incidence increases with age. However, whether the female sex or exposure to female hormones is a risk factor for NTM-PD development remains unclear ( 31 - 33 ). Additionally, the typical radiological features of NTM-PD include bronchiectasis, which is most prevalent in the right middle lobe or lingula; multifocal nodular or cavitary opacities; and multiple small nodules ( 3 , 34 , 35 ). Therefore, clinicians should recognize the high incidence of NTM-PD in patients with bronchiectasis and carefully assess clinical indicators in those with suspected cases ( 36 ), because a diagnosis of NTM-PD may necessitate antibiotic treatment and lead to significant changes in the clinical course.

What are the clinical outcomes in patients with bronchiectasis and an NTM phenotype? A recent study from the United States Bronchiectasis and NTM Research Registry compared the clinical outcomes between 1,549 patients (59%) with NTM and 1,085 patients (41%) without NTM at baseline ( 37 ). The NTM status was determined based on the responses to the questions in the case report form, which included details regarding the diagnosis of NTM, mycobacterial culture results confirming NTM, and treatments specific to NTM. Notably, outcomes, including exacerbations, hospitalizations, rate of lung function decline, and mortality rate, were comparable between the two groups during the 5-year follow-up ( 37 ). These results suggest that the NTM phenotype is not associated with poor outcomes in patients with bronchiectasis or that the outcomes may have been influenced by appropriate NTM-PD treatment.

P. aeruginosa phenotype The most well-characterized bronchiectasis phenotype is chronic bronchial infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (hereafter referred to as chronic P . aeruginosa infection or P . aeruginosa phenotype), which is associated with reduced health-related quality of life, more frequent exacerbations, higher rates of hospital admissions, and increased mortality ( 38 - 46 ). Therefore, chronic P . aeruginosa infection has been the focus of numerous randomized controlled trials evaluating inhaled antibiotics for bronchiectasis ( 47 ), with both existing and ongoing studies investigating strategies for eradicating this bacterium ( 48 , 49 ). Furthermore, international bronchiectasis guidelines recommend management strategies based on the status of chronic P . aeruginosa infection ( 13 , 15 ), and clinical trials on bronchiectasis often stratify participants based on the presence or absence of chronic P . aeruginosa infection ( 12 , 50 , 51 ).

Interestingly, chronic P . aeruginosa infections affect patients with bronchiectasis differently. A European multicenter study reported a high mortality risk in patients with bronchiectasis with a combination of P . aeruginosa infection and two or more exacerbations per year. In contrast, those with P . aeruginosa infection without frequent exacerbations had a favorable prognosis ( 38 ). These results suggest that the combination of P . aeruginosa infection and frequent exacerbations is associated with worse outcomes.

Frequent exacerbator phenotype The frequent exacerbator phenotype is also well-distinguished in patients with bronchiectasis, along with the P . aeruginosa phenotype. In a European multicenter cohort study (n=2,572), the baseline exacerbation frequency was categorized into zero, one, two, or three or more exacerbations per year, and long-term clinical outcomes were followed up for up to 5 years ( 52 , 53 ). Notably, a history of frequent exacerbations was the strongest predictor of future exacerbations, with the risk increasing in a dose-dependent manner according to the frequency of previous exacerbations. The incidence rate ratio for future exacerbation was 1.73 [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.47–2.02] for 1 exacerbation per year, 3.14 (95% CI: 2.70–3.66) for 2 exacerbations, and 5.97 (95% CI: 5.27–6.78) for three or more exacerbations ( 52 ). This phenotype was relatively stable over time, a pattern similar to that observed in COPD, wherein patients with frequent exacerbations are more susceptible to the subsequent exacerbations, independent of lung function ( 54 ).

As the frequent exacerbator phenotype is associated with increased hospitalization rates and higher 5-year mortality rates ( 52 ), the international bronchiectasis guidelines recommend management strategies aimed at preventing exacerbations ( 13 , 15 ). Furthermore, clinical trials on bronchiectasis have prioritized exacerbation as the primary outcome ( 12 , 51 , 55 ). The endotypes of bronchiectasis exacerbation, which may provide insights into the underlying biological mechanisms and potential therapeutic solutions, are discussed later in this review.

High symptom burden phenotype Current bronchiectasis guidelines regard the prevention of exacerbation and the management of daily symptoms as separate objectives. However, Gao et al. questioned this notion, noting that exacerbations worsen daily symptoms. Therefore, worse daily symptoms are a risk factor for exacerbation ( 56 ). The study revealed that the exacerbation risk increases by 10% for each 10-unit increase in the score on St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire, a validated health-related quality of life questionnaire ( 56 ). Furthermore, this observation was replicated in a prospective cohort study (n=436), which evaluated the symptom burden using the Quality-of-Life Bronchiectasis Respiratory Symptom Scale (QOL-B-RSS) ( 57 ). The baseline QOL-B-RSS score was associated with an increased risk of exacerbations (rate ratio: 1.3 for each 10-point decrease), hospitalizations (rate ratio: 1.2), and reduced time to the first exacerbation (hazard ratio: 1.1) over 12 months, even after adjusting for potential confounders such as exacerbation history ( 58 ).

As highly symptomatic patients with bronchiectasis have an increased risk of exacerbation, hospitalization, and poor clinical outcomes, the high symptom burden phenotype should be regarded as a distinct phenotype. Accumulating more evidence related to the management of highly symptomatic patients with bronchiectasis could lead to a shift in the paradigm of bronchiectasis management, potentially influencing future bronchiectasis guidelines ( 58 ).

Martinez-Garcia et al. previously proposed a clinical fingerprint for bronchiectasis, which comprised three components; activity (e.g., bronchial bacterial infection and number of annual exacerbations), impact (e.g., health-related quality of life and degree of dyspnea), and severity [e.g., forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and radiological extent]. This fingerprint may help physicians identify the clinical impact of the disease more precisely while taking into account the symptom burden ( 59 ).

Chronic airway diseases overlapped phenotype International bronchiectasis registries consistently reported that COPD and asthma are common in patients with bronchiectasis, ranging from 29–60%, although the registries enrolled patients whose primary diagnosis was bronchiectasis ( 19 - 24 ). The COPD-bronchiectasis overlap is clinically relevant because patients with this overlap are more likely to experience more severe symptoms, poorer quality of life, more frequent exacerbations, and increased mortality than those with COPD or bronchiectasis alone ( 60 - 64 ). Similarly, the asthma-bronchiectasis overlap has been associated with an increased risk of exacerbations ( 65 ), improved outcomes from ICS use, and reduced mortality, as indicated in a recent European Multicenter Bronchiectasis Audit and Research Collaboration (EMBARC) report ( 66 ).

However, there has been confusion over the diagnosis of COPD-bronchiectasis overlap because bronchiectasis is frequently observed in patients with COPD, and bronchiectasis can also cause airflow limitation ( 25 , 67 , 68 ). To address this diagnostic challenge, an international consensus proposed the standardized ROSE criteria {radiological bronchiectasis (R), obstruction [FEV1/FVC (forced vital capacity) ratio <0.7; O], symptoms (S), and exposure ≥10 pack-years of smoking (E)} ( 69 ). Significantly, a recent EMBARC study (n=16,730) revealed that 4,366 had a clinician-assigned COPD diagnosis; however, 22% of them did not have airflow obstruction, and 32% did not have a history of ≥10 pack-years of smoking ( 25 ). Hence, the ROSE criteria ( 25 , 69 ), a multi-omics study (discussed later) ( 18 ), and future studies would elucidate a more accurate diagnosis and reveal treatable traits in patients with COPD-bronchiectasis overlap.

Asthma-bronchiectasis overlap presents additional complexities in clinical practice. Diagnosing this overlap would be more challenging than the COPD-bronchiectasis overlap. Tests, such as bronchodilator reversibility, peak expiratory flow rate variability, fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) levels, and bronchial hyperresponsiveness, lack the sensitivity and specificity required for a definitive asthma diagnosis, although airflow obstruction to define COPD is relatively straightforward ( 70 , 71 ). Therefore, the misdiagnosis of asthma is prevalent in the general population, including those with bronchiectasis.

Disease labels are constructed to categorize patients for treatment. However, this classification system can be problematic for complex airway diseases. Approximately 50% of the patients with a single condition, such as COPD or asthma, may have bronchiectasis. Eventually, care for patients with severe and complex airway diseases may shift towards an endotype-driven approach ( 72 ). This strategy focuses on treating the underlying inflammatory pathways, such as Th2 airway inflammation, with medications, such as ICS or Th2 inflammation-targeting biologics, regardless of the primary diagnosis. Additionally, future treatments may specifically target neutrophilic inflammation, such as DPP-1 inhibitors, which are currently under clinical development for bronchiectasis ( 2 ).

Phenotypes identified by clustering studies Unsupervised cluster analyses based on clinical characteristics were also performed to determine the different bronchiectasis phenotypes. A European multicenter registry study (n=1,145) identified four clusters: severe disease with P . aeruginosa infection, chronic infection with other pathogens, sputum production without chronic bacterial infection, and dry bronchiectasis ( 73 ). Similarly, a Chinese study (n=148) identified four clusters: younger patients with mild and idiopathic bronchiectasis; older patients with severe post-infective bronchiectasis and P . aeruginosa infection; older patients with late-onset, severe idiopathic bronchiectasis; and older patients with moderate disease ( 74 ). Additionally, a Spanish study (n=468) revealed four clusters: young women with mild disease; overweight elderly women with mild bronchiectasis; elderly men with severe disease, chronic P . aeruginosa infection, airflow obstruction, and exacerbations; and older patients with severe disease and infrequent exacerbations ( 75 ).

Notably, patients with bronchiectasis and P . aeruginosa infection consistently exhibited distinct characteristics in all three studies ( 73 - 75 ), discussed earlier. However, other phenotypes identified by cluster analyses, including age of onset, idiopathic etiology, and overweight status, were too non-specific and had limited value in advancing the understanding of definitive bronchiectasis phenotypes.

Endotypes in bronchiectasis Neutrophilic inflammation Neutrophilic inflammation is a primary driver of bronchiectasis severity and progression, with high airway neutrophil levels associated with various chemokines, such as leukotriene B4, interleukin (IL)-8, IL-1β, and tumor necrosis factor-α ( 76 ). These neutrophils exhibit functional abnormalities, including excessive protease release, overwhelming anti-protease defense, and impaired pathogen clearance ( 77 , 78 ). Neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, which eliminates pathogens, can lead to tissue damage and inflammation. NETs release neutrophil elastase (NE), a key enzyme involved in tissue degranulation, impaired bacterial clearance, and mucus hypersecretion. Sputum NE levels correlate with exacerbation risk, lung function decline, and mortality ( 11 , 79 ). The NEATstik test is used to measure sputum NE levels and identify patients at a higher risk of exacerbation ( 80 ). Notably, a recent European multicenter study (n=13,484) demonstrated that sputum color, a more accessible measure of neutrophilic inflammation, was strongly associated with disease severity, lower FEV1, worse quality of life, and greater radiological severity of bronchiectasis ( 81 ).

DPP-1, crucial for activating serine proteases such as NE, is inhibited by drugs like brensocatib ( 78 ). The WILLOW trial demonstrated that brensocatib prolonged the time to the first exacerbation and reduced NE activity ( 12 ). Additionally, the ongoing phase 3 ASPEN trial showed a 20% reduction in the frequency of exacerbations (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04594369 ) ( 50 ), further confirming its efficacy. Another DPP-1 inhibitor, BI 1291583, demonstrated a numerical reduction in exacerbation risk ( 82 ) in an ongoing phase 2 trial ( NCT03696290 ). Identifying patients with bronchiectasis and increased neutrophilic inflammation based on NET or NE levels could enable targeted therapies. Further studies are needed to refine the markers of neutrophilic inflammatory endotypes and guide precision treatments.

Eosinophilic inflammation Although bronchiectasis has traditionally been regarded as a neutrophilic disease, it involves eosinophilic inflammation in some patients. One study reported blood eosinophilia in 22.6% of 1,007 patients, correlating with sputum eosinophilia and Th2 inflammation ( 83 ). High eosinophil counts are associated with increased disease severity and mortality, with eosinophilic patients experiencing shorter exacerbation-free periods after antibiotic treatment ( 83 ).

FeNO serves as a Th2 inflammation marker, with a Th2-high endotype noted in 31% of non-asthmatic bronchiectasis patients ( 84 ). This endotype is associated with higher disease severity and lower lung function. Identifying the eosinophilic endotype through blood and FeNO tests underscores the potential of precision medicine.

Monoclonal antibodies targeting the Th2 pathway, which have been proven effective in treating eosinophilic asthma, are yet to be tested in patients with bronchiectasis. Initial trials with inhaled fluticasone suggested improvements in the quality of life of patients with eosinophilic bronchiectasis ( 85 ). A case series indicated the benefits of mepolizumab and benralizumab in patients with high eosinophil counts ( 10 ). Preliminary trials, including an initial benralizumab trial ( NCT05006573 ), are underway to provide promising insights into the efficacy of these biologics in the treatment of bronchiectasis.

Systemic inflammation In bronchiectasis, inflammation is primarily localized in the lungs; however, systemic inflammation is observed during stable phases and exacerbations, correlating with disease severity. Clinical studies have shown that white blood cell and neutrophil counts increase during exacerbations, decrease with treatment, and align with radiological severity and lung function decline ( 86 , 87 ). A total of 802 patients from the Spanish Bronchiectasis Registry showed persistently high C-reactive protein (CRP) levels during severe exacerbations, predicting bacterial infections and poor outcomes following antibiotic treatment ( 88 ).

Fibrinogen, a coagulation cascade component, is a biomarker for the proinflammatory phenotype in COPD ( 89 ). In bronchiectasis, fibrinogen levels are also correlated with higher Bronchiectasis Severity Index; FACED (FEV1, age, chronic colonization, radiological extension, and dyspnea) score, and exacerbation risk ( 90 ). Saleh et al. analyzed 31 proteins in 90 patients and identified fibrinogen as a key severity marker associated with poor lung function and P . aeruginosa colonization ( 91 ). Additionally, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate, largely influenced by fibrinogen concentration, is correlated with exacerbation frequency and treatment response ( 86 ).

Desmosine, a product of elastin degradation by NE, is correlated with sputum elastase levels and severe exacerbations of bronchiectasis ( 79 ). It is linked to atherosclerosis and poorer post-myocardial infarction outcomes. Huang et al. further found that elevated serum desmosine levels were linked to increased cardiovascular mortality in these patients ( 92 ).

Systemic inflammation promotes platelet aggregation. In a study by Aliberti et al. ( 93 ), the occurrence of thrombocytosis in 1,771 patients with bronchiectasis was related to severe disease, poorer quality of life, increased frequency of exacerbations, and higher mortality at 3 and 5 years. Méndez et al. ( 94 ) reported elevated soluble P-selectin levels in patients with severe cases, indicating heightened platelet activation at baseline.

Cluster analyses that incorporate multiple systemic biomarkers may provide a more effective approach to characterizing patients with bronchiectasis compared with the measurement of individual biomarkers alone. Wang et al. ( 95 ) identified three distinct clusters according to the levels of systemic biomarkers, including neutrophils, eosinophils, lymphocyte counts, CRP, and hemoglobin, which exhibited significant correlations with disease severity. However, several clinical factors, such as comorbidities, affect systemic inflammatory markers. Therefore, we should understand that systemic inflammation exists in bronchiectasis, but it is challenging to recognize its clinical significance precisely and treat it as a treatable target, unlike airway inflammation.

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) AMPs are a diverse group of molecules that play a crucial role in host defense against microbial infections; however, they can exhibit pro-inflammatory properties in the context of chronic lung disease. Sibila et al. ( 96 ) found that frequent exacerbators with bronchiectasis exhibited dysregulated levels of sputum AMPs, characterized by elevated levels of LL-37 and decreased levels of secretory leukocyte peptidase inhibitors (SLPIs). Elevated LL-37 and diminished SLPI levels in the sputum were independently associated with disease severity, P . aeruginosa infection, and an increased risk of future exacerbations. Furthermore, cluster analysis conducted by Perea et al. demonstrated that patients could be classified according to their AMP levels, with the highest concentrations associated with the most severe disease presentations ( 97 ).

Endotypes identified by clustering studies Given the heterogeneity of the causes, clinical manifestations, and treatment responses in patients with bronchiectasis, multiple inflammatory endotypes have been identified and classified according to their distinct biological mechanisms. Choi et al. ( 98 ) recently delineated four inflammatory endotypes using unsupervised cluster analysis based on 20 sputum and 13 serum inflammatory markers: (I) milder neutrophilic inflammation, characterized by lower concentrations of inflammatory markers, reduced exacerbation rates, and less pronounced airway microbiome dysbiosis; (II) mixed neutrophilic and Th2 inflammation, defined by the presence of biomarkers such as IL-5, IL-8, and NE; (III) severe neutrophilic inflammation, characterized by elevated levels of IL-8, NE, and NETs, with both clusters 2 and 3 associated with increased exacerbation risk and Pseudomonas -enriched microbiome; and (IV) mixed epithelial and Th2 inflammation, characterized by presence of biomarkers such as IL-5, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, IL-6, and vascular endothelial growth factor. This endotype was associated with a Streptococcus -dominated microbiome and systemic inflammation. The associations between these specific inflammatory endotypes, infections, and clinical outcomes were further corroborated by previous evidence linking NE and microbial infections to poor outcomes. Additionally, severe disease has been observed in patients with eosinophilia, albeit with distinct microbiome profiles.

Regarding COPD-bronchiectasis overlap, Huang et al. ( 18 ) found that patients with this overlap exhibited distinct lung microbiota and host response profiles compared with patients with COPD alone, whose microbiota resembled that of patients with bronchiectasis. The authors proposed five endotypes based on clinical characteristics, sputum microbiome profiles, and protein markers that reflected potential “treatable traits”. These endotypes include (I) diverse-protective endotype: associated with the most favorable prognosis; (II) Haemophilus -proteolytic endotype: linked to Haemophilus infection, with tetracyclines as a potential treatment option; (III) infected-epithelial response endotype: characteristic of patients with bronchiectasis with gram-negative infections, likely benefiting from macrolide therapy; (IV) Proteobacteria -neutrophilic endotype: possibly responsive to macrolides due to similarities with bronchiectasis, including heightened neutrophil activation and NET formation; and (V) Th2 endotype: noted for its responsiveness to ICS or other therapies targeting Th2-mediated inflammation.

Taken together, precise endotype analysis that accounts for distinct causes and inflammatory profiles enhances clinical decision-making in the management of bronchiectasis. Microbiome Airway infections play a fundamental role in the pathogenesis of bronchiectasis. Bacterial infections have traditionally been attributed to pathogenic organisms. However, the introduction of next-generation sequencing has shifted this perspective, highlighting microbial dysbiosis, characterized by a loss of microbial diversity and the dominance of certain organisms, as a significant factor in disease progression ( 99 ).

Recent studies have revealed that bronchiectasis is often associated with a Proteobacteria -dominant microbiome, particularly featuring Pseudomonas , which is linked to more severe diseases and poorer clinical outcomes ( 98 , 100 ). This suggests that targeting specific microbial populations may offer potential avenues for intervention ( 100 ). Some patients exhibit a Firmicutes -dominant microbiome, such as Streptococci . The decline in commensal anti-inflammatory bacteria such as Rothia mucilaginosa has important clinical implications ( 101 ). Microbiomes also harbor resistome and antimicrobial resistance genes, which can guide the development of targeted therapeutic strategies ( 102 ). Additionally, the mycobiome, particularly of Aspergillus , is clinically relevant owing to its role in fungal sensitization and immune responses ( 103 ).

A key question remains whether reduced microbial diversity leads to increased risk of exacerbations and worsened outcomes due to the overgrowth of dominant pathogens or whether it is a result of repeated antibiotic treatments causing microbial depletion and subsequent colonization. Notably, approximately one-third of patients with bronchiectasis do not exhibit chronic infection; instead, they have a microbiome enriched with “commensals” such as Streptococcus , Veillonella , Prevotella , Rothia , and Neisseria ( 99 , 101 , 104 ). Understanding how these taxa may act as “pathobionts” under certain conditions is vital.

Future research should focus on the dynamics of microbial communities rather than evaluating isolated microbes. Investigating how the microbiome interacts with clinical, inflammatory, immunological, and metabolic factors may open new avenues for understanding and treating bronchiectasis.

Genetics Genetic investigations specific to bronchiectasis are limited. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is expected to uncover novel genetic etiologies in patients with idiopathic bronchiectasis. The Genetics Encoding Complex Ciliopathies of Bronchiectasis study, conducted by EMBARC, analyzed whole exome sequences from over 1,000 patients with idiopathic bronchiectasis. Preliminary data indicated that WGS detected PCD in 12% of patients with severe bronchiectasis and 7% of those not typically suspected of this condition ( 17 ).

Mannose-binding lectin, an essential component of the innate immune response, is commonly genetically deficient, and this deficiency is associated with increased disease severity, poor quality of life, higher exacerbation rates, and more frequent hospitalizations ( 105 ). Additionally, the secretion of α-1,2-fucosylated glycans, regulated by the secretor genotype, has emerged as a risk factor influencing infection type and disease progression ( 106 ).

As larger patient cohorts with linked biobanks are established, a more comprehensive understanding of the genetic factors that contribute to bronchiectasis endotypes is essential. Moreover, investigating the ethnic and geographical variations in genetic variants will provide valuable insights into their roles in the pathogenesis of bronchiectasis.

Endotypes of bronchiectasis exacerbation Bronchiectasis exacerbations have traditionally been regarded as bacterial infection-driven events; therefore, they are primarily managed with antibiotics ( 13 , 15 ). However, this simplistic view has been challenged by the heterogeneity of exacerbations, which can arise from various exogenous and endogenous factors that disrupt patient homeostasis.

Gao et al. ( 107 ) proposed that bronchiectasis exacerbations can be categorized into distinct types: bacterial, viral, bacterial/viral co-infection, eosinophilic, and unidentified types, each with unique microbiome and inflammatory profiles. They identified four exacerbation endotypes through an integrative approach that combined microbiome analysis, proteomics, and viral polymerase chain reaction: (I) a Pseudomonas -associated cluster, characterized by significant upregulation of neutrophil proteins such as ELANE (elastase), myeloperoxidase, and azurocidin; (II) a Haemophilus -associated cluster, marked by elevated levels of human defensins (defensin alpha 1/3); (III) an eosinophilic inflammation cluster associated with proteins like EZR, PYCARD, WHAG, and Galectin-10, indicating non-infective exacerbations; and (IV) a cluster defined by excessive mucus production and epithelial response, with high expression of MUC5AC, MUC5B, and PIGR, and a Streptococcus -dominated microbiome.

Understanding these exacerbation endotypes is critical for selecting suitable patients for clinical trials and developing precise treatment strategies. Ongoing research on biomarkers defining these endotypes is expected to enhance personalized prevention and therapy for bronchiectasis exacerbation.

Conclusions Toward precision medicine The heterogeneity of bronchiectasis poses significant challenges in disease management, complicating efforts to tailor treatments and improve patient outcomes. Although the concept of treatable traits in bronchiectasis provides a strategic approach to address this challenge, it often lacks critical biological insights into the underlying causal mechanisms that are essential for developing novel, targeted interventions. Insights gained from other lung conditions, such as asthma and COPD, highlight that integrating endophenotyping can significantly enhance the understanding of disease characteristics, thereby enabling the development of more precise and effective therapeutic strategies. In bronchiectasis, clinical phenotypes involve categorizing the disease based on patient characteristics; however, this process remains complex. Widely recognized clinical phenotypes, such as “NTM-PD”, “chronic P . aeruginosa infection”, “frequent exacerbator”, “high symptom burden”, and “chronic airway disease overlapped”, provide clear clinical relevance but only capture part of the disease’s complexity. Further phenotypic layers involve the analysis of radiographic patterns and the identification of underlying etiologies. However, clinical phenotyping alone is inadequate to fully encapsulate the complexity of the disease, which involves differences in severity, activity, and impact among different phenotypes.

Investigating molecular endotypes that evaluate the disease based on the underlying pathobiological mechanisms and treatment responses provides a more comprehensive understanding of bronchiectasis. This approach is exemplified by the identification of distinct inflammatory patterns, such as neutrophilic/NETS and eosinophilic/Th2 airway inflammation. Each clinical phenotype may encompass multiple endotypes, and a single endotype may be associated with multiple phenotypes. Identifying the therapeutic targets within these frameworks introduces the concept of “treatable traits”. Advancing endophenotyping in bronchiectasis, is therefore, vital for applying precision medicine strategies that more effectively tackle the considerable heterogeneity of the disease, ultimately enhancing patient outcomes.

For commercial reproduction rights and permissions contact permissions@ersnet.org Bronchiectasis is a heterogeneous chronic airway disease primarily driven by persistent infection, microbial dysbiosis and dysregulated host immunity. While culture-based microbiology has historically informed clinical management, advances in high-throughput sequencing and multi-omic technologies have transformed our understanding of the airway ecosystem, revealing that disease activity is shaped not only by individual pathogens, but by complex and dynamic host–microbe interactions. Despite the breadth of descriptive microbiome data, translation into clinically actionable diagnostics or therapies has been limited. Importantly, cross-sectional correlations between microbiota and inflammation do not establish cause and effect, underscoring the need to embed host–microbiome profiling within both longitudinal and interventional therapeutic trials. In this review, we critically appraise current microbial and host multi-omics research in bronchiectasis, integrating microbiome studies with host inflammatory, proteomic and immunophenotyping data. We highlight themes emerging across cohorts, including low microbial diversity, pathogen dominance, loss of commensal networks and neutrophil-driven inflammation, and discuss how these features align with biological endotypes associated with exacerbations and treatment response. Drawing on lessons from host-directed therapeutic successes, we examine translational roadblocks limiting microbiome-guided care. We further review emerging microbiome-modulating strategies such as pathogen-specific biologics, bacteriophage therapy, live biotherapeutic products, biofilm-targeting adjuncts and precision antibiotic stewardship. Finally, we propose a roadmap toward microbiome-informed precision medicine through harmonised methodologies, integration of host and microbial biomarkers into clinical trials, and embedding multi-omics pipelines within large international registries. Collectively, these advances have the potential to shift bronchiectasis research and clinical management towards rationally designed, precision medicine-driven therapeutic strategies.

It is a heterogeneous disease with genetic, infectious, airway and immune-mediated causes, although many cases remain idiopathic [ 4 – 6 ]. The disease process is driven by dominant infections with Gram-negative pathogens, notably Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Haemophilus influenzae [ 7 ], and primarily neutrophilic inflammation resulting in impaired mucociliary clearance and progressive tissue damage [ 8 – 10 ]. These processes reflect a complex interplay between microbial dysbiosis and host immune dysregulation in the airways resulting in a so-called “vicious vortex” [ 11 ].

Advances in high-throughput omics have driven translational progress in bronchiectasis, with large-scale airway and blood profiling enabling the identification of molecular endotypes and treatable traits [ 7 , 12 – 14 ]. These studies have highlighted novel targets, such as neutrophil serine proteases (NSPs) [ 11 , 15 , 16 ], and biomarker signatures now informing precision-medicine trials [ 7 ]. In parallel, trials of targeted anti-inflammatory drugs are underway [ 17 – 19 ]. In contrast, sequencing-based airway microbiome studies have largely been descriptive [ 20 – 24 ], and translating these findings into diagnostics or microbiome-directed therapies remains challenging. In this review, we critically evaluate bronchiectasis microbiome and host–pathogen research, highlighting the key translational barriers that continue to impede microbiome-guided care and outline a roadmap for moving from descriptive association studies toward mechanism-based, clinically actionable, precision therapeutics.

Microbial multi-omics in bronchiectasis: from description to function Culture-independent microbiology and multi-omic profiling have revealed that bronchiectasis is a disease shaped not simply by individual pathogens, but by dynamic interactions between the airway microbial community and host inflammatory responses. This section describes both the well-characterised cross-sectional features of bronchiectasis microbiology and the more translational concepts of host–microbe endotyping.

Cross-sectional microbial signatures In bronchiectasis, traditional culture-based sputum microbiology has repeatedly shown that pathogens such as P. aeruginosa are associated with worse clinical outcomes, but this approach underrepresents the complexity of the respiratory microbiome ( table 1 ) [ 9 , 25 ]. Culture-independent approaches, including 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, have now established a consistent cross-sectional signal whereby the airway microbiome in bronchiectasis is frequently characterised by reduced diversity, pathogen dominance and depletion of commensal taxa [ 20 , 26 , 27 ]. Shotgun metagenomics adds strain-level resolution and functional insight, including presence of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and resistome structures [ 25 , 28 – 30 ]. Recently, analysis of sputum metagenomes from participants in the European Bronchiectasis Registry (EMBARC) identified four microbial metacommunities/clusters using Dirichlet multinomial mixture modelling [ 25 ]. Two were pathogen-dominant, driven primarily by H. influenzae and P. aeruginosa , and were associated with lower α-diversity and greater disease severity. In addition, two commensal-enriched clusters were identified, one of which showed high microbial diversity with low interindividual variability and was dominated by diverse oral commensals, and the other displayed greater inter-individual heterogeneity or “personalised” metagenomes. Across these clusters, disease severity inversely correlated with microbial diversity and depletion of taxa was associated with less ecologically balanced airway communities, such as Neisseria , Fusobacterium and Eubacterium [ 25 ]. However, these findings do not imply that such taxa are uniformly protective; rather, it suggests loss of community structure and colonisation resistance, coupled with local immunomodulatory function, may sustain inflammation even without a single dominant pathogen. Pan-European metagenomic data further show marked geographic variation in airway microbiota and resistomes, suggesting that local ecological and antimicrobial pressures shape bronchiectasis heterogeneity and treatment response [ 30 ].

Longitudinal dynamics and functional ecology Integrative “multi-biome” analyses incorporating bacterial, viral and fungal communities are further redefining bronchiectasis ecology and suggest that the highest-risk patients exhibit simplified, antagonistic microbial networks centred on Pseudomonas , with network structure predicting exacerbations more accurately than microbial abundance alone [ 23 ]. Longitudinal 16S studies similarly show that bronchiectasis microbiomes are relatively stable within individuals during clinical stability, while exacerbations may reflect transient ecological destabilisation rather than wholesale taxonomic replacement [ 27 , 31 ]. Patients with persistently low diversity or simplified co-occurrence networks appear more prone to future decline and repeated exacerbation, supporting repeated sampling across clinical states in biomarker and therapeutic studies.

Multibiome ecology also includes pathobiont and fungal signals that do not fit a simple pathogen versus commensal dichotomy [ 32 ]. Taxa traditionally considered commensal, such as Neisseria spp. may behave as pathobionts in dysbiosis or altered host immunity [ 33 ]. In this setting, Neisseria -enriched communities have been associated with worse outcomes, including more frequent exacerbations and reduced lung function. Rather than Neisseria being intrinsically harmful in all settings, this suggests that pathogenic behaviour emerges when community balance and host control are disrupted [ 33 ]. Similarly, beyond allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, elevated Aspergillus -specific IgG and eosinophilic bronchiectasis define additional subgroups with worse lung function and more frequent, more severe exacerbations, highlighting that nonbacterial components of the airway ecosystem also shape clinically relevant endotypes [ 34 ].

Importantly, descriptive sequencing findings are increasingly supported by translational studies showing that local commensals can attenuate airway inflammation and pathogen behaviour. G oeteyn et al . [ 35 ] demonstrated that selected lung commensals suppress NF-κB activation and interleukin (IL)-8 production in a three-dimensional epithelial model, while G rassi et al . [ 36 ] showed that several Prevotella isolates reduced P. aeruginosa biofilm formation and altered virulence-associated behaviour. Moreover, these data provide a mechanistic rationale for future microbiome-preserving or microbiome-restorative therapeutic approaches.

Host inflammatory endotypes Linking microbial patterns to host immunity has enabled more biologically grounded frameworks for disease endotyping ( figure 1 ). Inflammatory profiles characterised by elevated sputum neutrophil elastase (NE), IL-8 [ 37 ] and IL-1β [ 38 ] track closely with microbial composition and exacerbation risk [ 39 ]. In a multicentre study, C hoi et al . [ 40 ] identified bronchiectasis endotypes defined by cytokine clustering, showing that neutrophilic and type 2 inflammation were associated with Pseudomonas dominance, reduced diversity and frequent exacerbation. Proteomic profiling further demonstrated that neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) proteins are among the most robust biomarkers of disease severity, correlating with exacerbation frequency, hospitalisation and mortality [ 41 ].

Extending this host–microbe paradigm, a recent study used an integrated multiparameter/multi-methods approach across different chronic lung diseases and defined two cross-disease airway endotypes: a “neutrophilic” cluster characterised by high neutrophil elastase, reduced α-diversity, enriched Proteobacteria and abnormal sputum rheology, contrasted with a “Th2/mucin-rich” cluster. Bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis (CF) were highly enriched in the neutrophilic endotype, reinforcing that functional microbial–host interactions, rather than taxonomy alone, underpin clinically relevant airway phenotypes [ 42 ]. Consistent with this neutrophil-dominant endotype, NE levels were highest in the lobes with most dilated airways and strongly correlated with sputum levels (r=0.84), linking localised airway injury to global airway biomarkers and validating sputum NE as a regional surrogate [ 43 ].

These observations connecting microbial dysbiosis, neutrophil activation, and biofilm formation illustrates a self-perpetuating infection–inflammation cycle. Accordingly, functional traits such as biofilm formation, ARG expression and production of immunomodulatory microbial metabolites may better explain clinical trajectories than taxonomy alone [ 28 ].

Complementing airway-focused omics, emerging immunophenotyping suggest that bronchiectasis, particularly with chronic P. aeruginosa infection, is accompanied by systemic immune dysregulation. Chronic airway infection and inflammation appear to extend beyond the lung, shaping circulating innate and adaptative profiles in ways that reflect a less activated and potentially maladaptive peripheral immune state. In one recent study, lower circulating lymphocytes and B-cells reduced human leukocyte antigen-DR + activated CD4 + /CD8 + T-cells and regulatory T-cells, altered Th17-related balance and, among those with chronic P. aeruginosa infection, higher neutrophils and CD14 + monocytes were observed with a persistently tolerant/less-active peripheral profile over 12 months [ 44 ]. Importantly, these systemic immune signatures may mirror airway disease activity and severity, highlighting blood-based biomarkers as surrogates of pulmonary disease burden, as recently demonstrated in CF [ 45 ].

Emerging functional readouts Metatranscriptomic data in bronchiectasis are still limited and represented more sparsely than bacterial, viral and fungal sequencing studies, but offer the important advantage of resolving active microbial behaviour rather than organism presence alone [ 46 ]. Proteomic and metabolomic studies are also emerging [ 47 – 50 ], with early data linking lipid mediators with bacterial abundance, and eosinophilic inflammation to clinically relevant phenotypes [ 51 ]. Extending beyond sputum, nasopharyngeal microbiome profiling has been proposed as a more accessible sampling site that may relate to mucociliary dysfunction, microbial imbalance and exacerbation risk [ 52 ], although upper and lower airway communities can be distinct and their concordance may depend on factors such as disease severity, limiting the extent to which the upper airway can be treated as a surrogate. These data mark a shift from descriptive microbiology toward actionable host–microbe endotypes, while also illustrating the remaining challenge of distinguishing association from causation.

From endotypes to targeted therapy Finally, bronchiectasis research is drawing on advances from other chronic airway diseases such as asthma [ 53 , 54 ] and COPD [ 55 , 56 ], where use of integrated host multi-omics and a precision medicine approach have combined to inform the development of targeted therapies. In bronchiectasis, this is already evident in the emergence of NSP pathway inhibitors [ 11 , 57 ] and IL-33-directed strategies [ 58 ], both of which stem from biologically defined inflammatory endotypes. These advances suggest that bronchiectasis is beginning to shift from descriptive microbiology toward actionable host–microbe endotypes, raising the possibility that integrated microbial and immune signatures could be used to guide targeted therapy ( figure 1 ). As more cohorts accumulate, it should become possible to build an “omics atlas” that links sputum microbiome, host transcriptomic/proteomic and metabolomic features to clinical records, which would then enable externally validated endotypes to become therapeutically actionable at the bedside.

Overcoming translational barriers: integrating host and microbiome omics in bronchiectasis Translating microbiome science into clinically useful tools will require more than ongoing detailed descriptive datasets. In bronchiectasis, progress is limited not only by biological and methodological heterogeneity, but also by the persistent gaps between association and therapeutic action. This section considers the major barriers to clinical translation.

Methodological and sampling barriers Bronchiectasis exemplifies a biologically complex disorder in which patient heterogeneity hampers biomarker discovery and clinical translation ( figure 1 ). Individual patients display distinct airway communities with some maintaining relatively stable microbiomes over years, whereas others experience abrupt shifts in dominant taxa. Disease expression is also spatially heterogeneous, with some lobes chronically infected or dilated while others remain relatively preserved, creating region-specific microbial and inflammatory environments [ 59 ]. Consequently, a single sputum sample may capture only a partial snapshot of the airway ecosystem, and intrapatient variability limits straightforward correlations between microbiome composition and disease severity.

Technical variability further compounds this challenge. There is no consensus on standardised airway sampling or processing in bronchiectasis research. Studies differ in sample type (sputum, throat swabs or bronchoalveolar lavage), pre-analytical handling, extraction method, primer choice and sequencing platform. Each methodological choice can alter the resulting community profiles, while the use of nonstandardised bioinformatic pipelines further limit reproducibility. Interpretation is further complicated by the risk of contamination of lower airway samples from the upper aerodigestive tract, oral taxa, or environmental and reagent sources, particularly in low-biomass specimens where distinguishing true biological signal from contamination is difficult [ 60 , 61 ]. The absence of unified data standards, particularly inconsistent reporting of antibiotic exposure, inhaled therapy and clinical scores, prevents robust meta-analysis and hinders comparison across cohorts. As noted in recent microbiome commentaries, this field suffers from “missing metadata” and inconsistent analytical frameworks [ 62 ], resulting in poor (cross-study) reproducibility across cohorts. Even when collection and sequencing are standardised, between-site differences in airway clearance practice, antibiotic stewardship and clinical management may remain important sources of variation in multicentre studies.

From molecular endotypes to theratypes CF provides a useful example of how deep biological profiling can support precision therapy and personalised medicine. Its monogenic aetiology enabled the development of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators, most notably the triple combination elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor [ 63 ], and more recently vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor [ 64 ], that target the underlying CFTR protein defect, thereby improving mucus properties, microbiome composition and airway inflammation 65 – 69 ]. Initially, CFTR modulators were only approved for patients with the common F508del mutation, leaving many with rare CFTR variants untreated. However, in vitro and in vivo testing has shown that many non-F508del variants respond to CFTR modulators [ 70 , 71 ]. According to this theratyping concept, patients are now classified by their response to targeted therapy, rather than CFTR genotype alone [ 72 , 73 ].

In contrast, bronchiectasis is a multifactorial syndrome lacking a single unifying genetic driver ( figure 1 ). Rather than relying on genotype-based theratyping, future treatment paradigms may employ multi-omic theratypes defined by integrated host–microbe signatures. For example, a Pseudomonas- dominant, neutrophil-high endotype could warrant a distinct therapeutic approach compared to a mixed oral-commensal, or eosinophilic endotype. Preliminary sputum and blood cytokine studies have begun to define such molecular endotypes [ 40 ]; however, these remain descriptive and have not yet informed therapeutic decisions. Achieving a framework for “bronchiectasis theratyping” will require the integration of host and microbial omics linked to treatment outcomes, a considerably more complex endeavour than the single-gene paradigm applicable in CF.

Why association is insufficient Beyond methodology, the most important translational barrier lies in moving from population-level associations to individual clinical prediction and causal inference. While numerous studies link Pseudomonas dominance and low microbial diversity to exacerbation risk, no airway microbiome signature has yet matured into a validated diagnostic or prognostic tool. Associations between diversity metrics and lung function decline hint at predictive value [ 27 ], but thresholds and clinical cut-offs remain undefined. Most studies remain cross-sectional or observational, unable to meet the Bradford Hill criteria for causation, such as temporality or biological gradient [ 74 ].

To date, published host-directed bronchiectasis trials have mainly focused on clinical and inflammatory outcomes [ 16 , 18 , 19 , 75 ], with embedded microbiome sequencing rarely reported outside of antibiotic trials [ 76 – 79 ]. If the field is to move beyond increasingly accurate prediction models, future studies must prioritise bidirectional interventional designs through manipulating host pathways and observing microbiome consequences, as well as manipulating the microbiome and measuring host inflammatory responses. Omics approaches should therefore be viewed not as replacements for conventional clinical assessment, but as complementary tools capable of uncovering actionable mechanisms underpinning clinical phenotypes.

From prediction to intervention Importantly, complex omics profiles will need to complement pragmatic clinical predictors. Recent clinical evidence shows that even simple symptom-based measures may outperform current biomarker strategies. For example, a large international cohort noted that daily symptom burden (Quality-of-Life Bronchiectasis Respiratory Symptom Scale) independently predicted future exacerbations and that highly symptomatic patients, despite infrequent prior exacerbations, derived similar benefit from macrolide therapy as “traditional” frequent exacerbators [ 80 ]. Similarly, data from the iBEST (iABC Bronchiectasis Efficacy Study with TIP) cohort indicate that baseline lung function was a key determinant of treatment response [ 76 ], raising an important question of whether readily available clinical metrics may, in some contexts, outperform complex omics-based stratification. These findings underscore a critical translational gap: although lung function and symptom burden may serve as pragmatic predictors of treatment response, they fail to elucidate the underlying biological heterogeneity among patients or inform strategies to optimise therapies and extend them to novel targets. To expand beyond readily available clinical tools for deep phenotyping, establishing causal mechanisms will require longitudinal sampling with standardised metadata and experimental validation in models that can disentangle infection dynamics from host response. Omics approaches should be regarded not as replacements for conventional clinical assessment, but as complementary tools that provide molecular level insights necessary to uncover actionable mechanisms underlying observable clinical phenotypes.

Translating airway microbiome data into therapeutic guidance is also problematic. Although in principle, resistome data could personalise antibiotic selection, clinical translation remains limited. In CF, systematic reviews suggest that the relationship between standard in vitro susceptibility testing and clinical response is inconsistent across studies [ 81 ]. More broadly, future analyses should move beyond organism abundance alone towards network-level interaction and damage-response frameworks that better reflect which communities are driving clinically relevant injury. The CFMATTERS trial further exemplifies this translational gap: Pseudomonas -positive CF participants received either guideline recommended dual intravenous antibiotic therapy or guideline therapy plus an additional microbiome-directed antibiotic. However, the addition of a third antibiotic, guided by sputum microbiome analysis, did not improve clinical outcomes compared to standard dual therapy; in fact, patients in this group experienced more i.v. antibiotic days [ 82 ]. This negative result should not be interpreted as evidence against microbiome-guided therapy, rather, it highlights the limitations of pairing descriptive abundance data with broad-spectrum antibiotics. The same framework may prove more informative when matched to narrower pathogen-directed strategies such as phages, monoclonal antibodies or bacteriocins. Indeed, in bronchiectasis, post hoc analyses of the ORBIT-3 and ORBIT-4 inhaled ciprofloxacin trials suggest that integrated host–microbiome endotypes may help to identify subgroups more likely to benefit from inhaled antibiotics such as Pseudomonas -colonised patients with distinct microbiota and inflammatory profiles that explained differential drug efficacy [ 79 ]. Candidate biomarkers such as NE, Rothia abundance and/or lymphocyte specific protein 1 expression may serve as stratification tools for inhaled antibiotic trials.

Emerging therapeutic directions in microbiome modulation As the limitations of conventional therapies become clearer, attention is turning to strategies that directly or indirectly reshape the airway microbiome in bronchiectasis, and these are explored in this section ( figure 2 ) [ 83 – 88 ].

Pathogen-directed and microbiome-sparing strategies There is growing interest in therapies that selectively target pathogens while preserving commensals. Bacteriophage therapy remains conceptually attractive for refractory P. aeruginosa infection, but currently the clinical signal is mixed. Small CF and non-CF bronchiectasis series (∼30 patients) have reported feasibility and favourable safety and microbiological responses [ 89 ], with minimal adverse events and occasional bacterial regrowth or phage neutralisation [ 90 ]. Larger compassionate-use studies in drug-resistant nontuberculous mycobacteria, frequent in bronchiectasis, report clinical improvement in over half of patients without phage-related toxicity and no emergence of phage resistance [ 91 ]. However, publicly available data for the phase 2 trial (Tailwind), evaluating AP-PA02, an inhaled multiphage therapeutic, indicated that pre-specified efficacy analyses of the individual bronchiectasis cohorts did not show a significant difference versus placebo, although post hoc pooled analyses suggested reduced P. aeruginosa burden [ 92 ]. Similarly, BiomX discontinued its BX004 phase 2b programme after safety review and internal analysis of unexpectedly high adverse-event rates [ 93 ]. These developments indicate that while initial reports were favourable, they have not yet translated into definitive controlled-trial evidence.

However, other microbiome-sparing strategies may be closer to clinical translation. Gremubamab, a bispecific monoclonal antibody targeting the P. aeruginosa virulence factors PcrV, and Psl involved in biofilm formation [ 94 – 97 ], shows broad activity across clinical isolates with reduced airway bacterial load and improved patient-reported quality of life in patients with bronchiectasis [ 98 , 99 ]. Engineered bacteriocins, including chimeric pyocins, offer another precision antimicrobial approach for strain-specific eradication of multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas [ 100 ] that may preserve other taxa.

Another emerging strategy that may bridge infection and inflammation is inhaled polyvalent IgG. CSL787 is a nebulised IgG formulation with potential anti-infective, anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects; early phase 1 data reported a favourable safety profile with reductions in sputum bacterial counts [ 101 ], and a phase 2b bronchiectasis study is underway [ 102 ].

Microbiome-restorative strategies An alternative paradigm focuses on re-establishing a protective microbial equilibrium. Evidence from CF and asthma suggests that gut–lung axis modulation through probiotics can influence airway inflammation and infection risk [ 103 ]. Building on this, live biotherapeutic products are being developed for direct airway delivery [ 104 – 106 ]. Inhaled Lactobacillus formulations have shown efficacy in pre-clinical models of neutrophilic lung injury occurring in bronchopulmonary dysplasia and COPD, improving lung architecture, reducing neutrophilic influx and suppressing matrix metalloproteinase-9/acetylated proline-glycine-proline signalling [ 105 ]. This concept is also supported by a recent study in β-epithelial sodium channel (βENaC)-Tg mice that share key features with CF and bronchiectasis [ 107 ], including impaired mucociliary clearance, mucus plugging, chronic neutrophilic inflammation and airway dysbiosis [ 108 – 110 ]. This study showed that therapeutic targeting of dysbiosis by intrapulmonary treatment with Ligilactobacillus murinus ( L. murinus SMH17), an endogenous probiotic bacterium isolated from the lungs of wild-type mice, reduces airway inflammation and mucus plugging in βENaC-Tg mice [ 107 ]. Although trials in patients with bronchiectasis are not yet available, these data provide proof of principle for respiratory probiotics or synbiotic (probiotic plus prebiotic) regimens aimed at rebalancing the airway microbiota, reducing inflammation and restoring airway homeostasis in muco-obstructive lung diseases.

Airway habitat- and biofilm-modifying adjuncts Airway clearance remains central to bronchiectasis care, with strategies targeting mucus properties or biofilm structure potentially reshaping airway microbiota. While recombinant DNase (dornase α) improves outcomes in CF, a large randomised controlled trial in non-CF bronchiectasis showed worsened lung function and poor tolerability, probably reflecting differences in mucus composition [ 111 ]. In CF, airway secretions are generally highly enriched in extracellular DNA and actin derived from profound neutrophilic inflammation and NET formation [ 112 , 113 ], allowing DNase to work as an effective mucolytic. In contrast, mucus in bronchiectasis is more heterogeneous and often predominantly mucin- and protein-rich, with comparatively lower extracellular DNA burden [ 41 , 57 , 114 ], such that DNase may have less effect on mucus viscoelasticity and clearance. In patients with low or early neutrophilic inflammation, NETs may retain protective antimicrobial roles, and indiscriminate NET degradation could impair host defence. In contrast, neutrophil-high bronchiectasis endotypes more closely resemble CF and may exhibit DNase-responsive mucus properties [ 42 , 115 ]. Hypertonic saline (7%) improves mucus hydration and short-term clearance [ 116 – 118 ], but longer studies [ 119 ] including the CLEAR study [ 120 ] did not demonstrate a clear reduction in exacerbations or microbial burden.

Nonetheless, these interventions may remain important to microbiome science, as they can reshape the airway microenvironment ( i.e. mucus concentration, biofilm architecture, oxygen diffusion and/or antibiotic penetration). Promising emerging mucolytic or biofilm-disrupting therapies include N-acetylcysteine and novel reducing agents such as fexlamose [ 121 , 122 ], which is now in phase II trial in COPD [ 123 ]. Mucinases, surfactant peptides and enzymatic cocktails combining DNase, proteases or alginate lyase are being evaluated for their ability to disperse biofilms and improve antibiotic penetration [ 124 ]. However, at present, such approaches should be viewed primarily as airway habitat modifiers pending mechanistic studies with paired host–microbiome readouts.

Precision antibiotic stewardship Precision antibiotic stewardship represents another development in microbiome modulation. Chronic bronchiectatic airways harbour diverse ARGs accumulated through repeated exposure to broad-spectrum antibiotics. Metagenomic studies show that Pseudomonas -dominated microbiomes carry high multidrug-resistance gene diversity, whereas Haemophilus -predominant communities contain narrower β-lactamase combinations [ 125 ]. Rapid DNA-based resistome profiling could inform antibiotic selection, preserving beneficial commensals while minimising selection pressure, as compared to the limitations of antimicrobial susceptibility testing [ 126 ]. Indeed, ARG abundance correlates strongly with inflammation and disease severity [ 125 ]. However, implementation remains challenging as even guideline-concordant antibiotic use enriches efflux pump and β-lactamase genes, as shown in recent metagenomic analyses [ 31 ]. Moreover, sequencing cannot capture antibiotic penetration, biofilm tolerance or adaptive resistance under treatment. Stewardship models will therefore need to integrate functional resistome data and clinical context rather than taxonomy alone.

Host-directed therapies and integrated readouts Although most microbiome-directed therapies remain early-stage, host-directed studies from CF with inhaled phage [ 127 , 128 ], emerging antivirulence platforms [ 129 ] and COPD with combination of anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial strategies [ 130 , 131 ] already offer important translational lessons. Discovery of NE as a key mediator and driver of bronchiectasis pathogenesis led to the development and clinical testing of inhibitors of dipeptidyl peptidase-1 (DPP-1, also known as cathepsin C), an enzyme essential for intracellular activation of the NSPs, NE, proteinase 3, and cathepsin G [ 11 ]. DPP-1 inhibitors prevent the release of active NSPs from neutrophils in the airways, thereby attenuating downstream tissue injury and inflammation [ 11 , 57 ]. This concept has been validated across multiple independent clinical trials, including brensocatib (WILLOW/ASPEN) [ 16 , 75 ], verducatib (BI 1291583) (AIRLEAF) [ 18 ], and florensocatib (HSK31858) (SAVE-BE/HOPE-BE) [ 19 , 132 ], demonstrating consistent reductions in NSP activity and clinically meaningful improvements in exacerbation outcomes. Brensocatib became the first licensed therapy in this class in August 2025 [ 16 ].

Similarly, IL-33-targeted biologics, now in early-phase bronchiectasis trials, derive directly from omics-defined inflammatory endotypes. IL-33 is an epithelial-derived alarmin released in response to airway injury and infection and has been implicated in driving type 2 inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and airway remodelling in airway diseases [ 133 – 136 ] including asthma and COPD [ 135 , 136 ], providing a mechanistic rationale for therapeutic targeting in IL-33-high endotypes in bronchiectasis [ 58 ]. While trial results are pending for use of anti-IL-33 monoclonal antibodies in bronchiectasis [ 137 ], the effort reflects how host multi-omic endotypes, such as “neutrophil-high” versus “IL-33-high”, can stratify patients for targeted therapy. Multilayer analyses of sputum from participants in the phase 2 WILLOW trial showed that brensocatib produced broad immunomodulatory effects, including increased antimicrobial peptides (secretory leukoproteinase inhibitor and α-defensin-3), reduced MUC5AC expression and remodelling of airway cytokine networks, demonstrating that inhibition of NSP activity reshapes the airway milieu [ 75 ]. Whether such changes are accompanied by meaningful shifts in microbiome structure remains largely unknown as embedded sequencing has rarely been reported. This should be viewed as a missed opportunity. Future host-directed and microbiome-directed trials should routinely integrate microbial, resistome and host-response end-points to determine not only whether a therapy works, but to provide mechanistic insight into how it works.

Gremubamab and planned inhaled live biotherapeutic product studies represent the first wave of more targeted microbiome interventions. Yet, the mixed results of PROMIS-I/II trials with inhaled colistimethate underline how variable trial outcomes can be, even in apparently well-defined subgroups [ 138 ]. Pre-clinical co-clinical models, including ex vivo bronchiectasis sputum culture [ 139 ], may help bridge this gap by testing how candidate bacteriocins, biologics or live biotherapeutics interact with microbial communities before or alongside clinical studies.

A roadmap for bringing microbiome science to the clinic A route to translation will require moving beyond cross-sectional association studies toward a staged framework that links biological discovery and validation, mechanistic testing and interventional application. The following roadmap outlines how microbiome and host multi-omics can be developed into clinically useful endotypes and, ultimately the potential for precision therapeutics in bronchiectasis ( figure 3 ).

Defining clinically useful endotypes Integrated host–microbiome profiling is beginning to define clinically actionable bronchiectasis endotypes. Combined sputum proteomic and microbiome analyses identify Proteobacteria-rich, neutrophilic, MUC5AC-high profiles alongside commensal-rich, anti-protease-dominant states [ 140 ]. Sputum metagenomics further distinguishes pathogen-dominant and commensal-depleted community states with distinct resistome signatures [ 125 ]. Among currently available candidates, sputum NE, NET-associated proteins, pathogen dominance (particularly Pseudomonas ) and certain microbial signatures (such as Rothia depletion) appear the most immediately translatable, as they reproducibly associate with exacerbation risk and in some settings even treatment response [ 22 ].

Longitudinal and interventional study design Moving from association to mechanism requires repeated sampling across stability, exacerbation, treatment and recovery. Integrative microbiomics show that exacerbations coincide with transient network simplification and loss of co-occurrence complexity, and that network topology may be more informative than relative abundance alone [ 23 ]. Long-term 16S surveillance similarly suggests that individual microbiomes can be remarkably stable, but persistently low diversity carries prognostic information [ 27 ]. The next generation of studies should therefore combine longitudinal microbial profiling with airway transcriptomic, proteomic and/or metabolomic readouts to clarify temporality and causality.

What should count as a microbiome end-point Incorporating microbiome and resistome outcomes into interventional trials is a critical next step. The landmark Bronchiectasis and Low-dose Erythromycin Study (BLESS) trial illustrates this approach, in which 12 months of erythromycin versus placebo induced significant shifts in sputum microbiota composition, including depleting H. influenzae and P. aeruginosa enrichment in previously chronically infected patients, yet exacerbation rates still decreased [ 77 ]. This does not necessarily contradict the association between dominant pathogens and worse disease severity. Rather, it illustrates that relative abundance shifts during therapy must be interpreted in ecological and clinical context, since suppression of competing taxa, immunomodulatory effects and altered network structure may coexist with short-term clinical benefit. This issue is further complicated by the fact that most microbiome datasets are compositional and changes in relative abundance do not necessarily reflect changes in absolute microbial burden [ 141 ]. Accordingly, apparent increases in a given organism may arise from loss of surrounding community members rather than true expansion [ 142 , 143 ], highlighting the importance of quantitative approaches to estimate absolute abundance in future interventional studies. However, defining what constitutes a clinically meaningful microbiome change remains challenging [ 144 ]. Diversity indices and relative abundances are variable and lack standardised clinical thresholds. An important unmet need is the definition of a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for microbiome outcomes, whether framed as changes in diversity, absolute pathogen burden and/or functional capacity, which can then be associated to patient-centred clinical end-points ( i.e. exacerbations, lung function decline, quality of life). Early-phase trials could therefore treat microbiome shifts as exploratory end-points by assessing multiple metrics (α/β diversity, specific taxa, resistome counts) alongside clinical outcomes while later-phase studies pre-specify microbiome MCIDs once biologically and clinically validated cut-offs are established [ 145 ].

Registry-scale translation and sources of variation Bringing microbiome-informed diagnostics and therapies into clinical practice requires alignment with regulatory frameworks for biologics and companion diagnostics. EMBARC [ 146 ] and related collaborations [ 147 ] provide the scale necessary for validation, but standardisation must extend beyond sample processing and bioinformatics to capture site-level differences in background therapies, antibiotic stewardship, airway-clearance practice and routine patient management. Embedding microbiome science within large registries and adaptive trial platforms, such as AIR-NET, offers a practical bridge from discovery to precision, endotype-driven bronchiectasis care [ 148 ].

Conclusions and future directions The next phase of bronchiectasis microbiome research must prioritise mechanism over further descriptive studies. Repeated sampling across clinical states, integrated within interventional studies, will be essential if the field is to move from association to causation. Just as importantly, future trials should routinely incorporate microbial, resistome and host biomarker end-points so that they can define not only whether an intervention works, but how it reshapes the airway ecosystem to enable regeneration and restore homeostasis. These studies should also consider integrating metagenomics with metatranscriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic readouts to distinguish which organisms are merely present from those which are biologically active and functionally relevant at key clinical time points. The greatest advances are now more likely to come from carefully designed mechanistic interventions, longitudinal sampling frameworks and harmonised translational infrastructure than from increasingly large cross-sectional datasets in isolation. With this shift, the airway microbiome can move beyond being a descriptive correlate of disease and become a practical component of precision therapeutics in bronchiectasis.

Bronchiectasis is a heterogeneous chronic respiratory disease characterised by permanent bronchial dilation, daily productive cough and frequent exacerbations [ 1 ]. In recent years, the understanding of bronchiectasis has evolved beyond the paradigm of recurrent infections and structural lung damage. Systemic inflammation and coexisting comorbidities are now recognised as integral components of disease pathophysiology [ 2 – 4 ]. Moreover, patients increasingly emphasise the need for personalised and flexible management strategies, pointing out the limitations of a one-size-fits-all approach [ 5 ]. Bronchiectasis has multiple potential causes, and a systematic aetiological evaluation to identify coexisting conditions is recommended, as distinct aetiologies may require specific treatments [ 6 ]. This perspective has led to the concept of treatable traits (TTs), originally introduced in COPD and asthma, and now extended to bronchiectasis [ 7 , 8 ]. TTs refer to clinically relevant, identifiable, and modifiable disease phenotypes, comorbidities, or underlying biological mechanisms (endotypes). While current guidelines provide management strategies involving antibiotics, pulmonary rehabilitation, and airway clearance, they do not adequately address comorbidities, lifestyle, or psychological health [ 9 , 10 ]. Limited data regarding the prevalence and distribution of TTs in bronchiectasis are available. Thus, the current study aimed to identify and characterise TTs in adults with bronchiectasis.

This was a secondary analysis of three prospective, observational studies conducted at the Bronchiectasis Programmes of the IRCCS San Gerardo dei Tintori, Monza, Italy (2012–2016), IRCCS Fondazione Cà Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Milan (2016–2020), and IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Milan (2021–2025), following a common study protocol. All studies received ethical approval from the respective institutional review boards, and informed consent was obtained from all patients.

Consecutive adults (≥18 years) with clinically and radiologically confirmed bronchiectasis were included, defined as bronchial dilation in ≥1 lobe along with compatible symptoms. Patients with cystic fibrosis or traction bronchiectasis secondary to interstitial lung diseases were excluded.

Clinical, laboratory, microbiological and radiological data were collected according to local standard operating procedures and the 2010/2019 British Thoracic Society and 2017 European Respiratory Society guidelines [ 9 , 10 ]. A total of 28 TTs were assessed across four domains at the time patients were referred to the bronchiectasis programmes: pulmonary traits, extrapulmonary comorbidities, aetiological diseases and lifestyle risk factors [ 8 ]. The primary endpoint of this study was to determine the prevalence of TTs in adults with bronchiectasis. The secondary endpoint was to compare the distribution of these TTs across centres, acknowledging that each centre represents a different time frame in the evolution of bronchiectasis care, reflecting modifications in clinical practice through the years. All analyses were performed using STATA v18.

A total of 1614 patients were included in this study: 574 from Humanitas (median (interquartile range (IQR)) age: 63 (54–70) years, 75% female), 700 from Policlinico (median (IQR) age: 62 (48–71) years, 77% female), and 340 from San Gerardo (median (IQR) age: 69 (58–75) years, 61.2% female). The median (IQR) bronchiectasis severity index (BSI) was 5.0 (3.0–8.0) at Humanitas, 5.5 (3.0–9.0) at Policlinico, and 6.0 (4.0–9.0) at San Gerardo, with 18.4%, 26.2%, and 29.4% classified as severe (BSI ≥9), respectively. Median (IQR) body mass index was 21.0 (19.0–23.5) at Humanitas, 21.4 (19.1–24.1) at Policlinico, and 22.6 (18.8–25.8) at San Gerardo. The distribution of the 28 TT across the three centres is shown in figure 1 . Chronic bacterial infection was observed in 25.3% at Humanitas, 34.9% at Policlinico, and 28.2% at San Gerardo. Airway clearance techniques were used by 50.5%, 65.7%, and 36.8%, respectively. Median (IQR) forced expiratory volume in 1 s % predicted was 86 (71–98) at Humanitas, 86 (69–101) at Policlinico, and 83 (61–102) at San Gerardo.
